bp: Local government meetings create records of what was discussed and decided, but those records are not written for easy public reading. A citizen who wants to know what happened about a street project, school issue, budget item, or permit may have to search through long formal minutes whose language is dense and procedural. This paper serves that public-access problem. It focuses on European Portuguese municipal meeting minutes and asks how a machine could produce a short summary for each discussion subject, not merely one broad summary of an entire meeting. The immediate contribution is a dataset, CitiLink-Summ: 120 municipal documents paired with 2,880 manually written summaries. That matters because automatic summarizers need examples of what a good short version should preserve. In this setting, the useful output is not decorative prose. It is a compact guide that helps citizens and researchers navigate local decisions without reading every formal record in full.
wh: The hard part is that municipal minutes are long because meetings are long and because public records must preserve procedure, speakers, agenda items, and decisions. A useful summary must compress that material while keeping the point of a specific discussion subject. If the system keeps too much wording, citizens still face the original navigation problem. If it cuts too much, it may lose the decision, the object being discussed, or the reason the subject mattered. The paper also works in a low-resource language setting. European Portuguese has less task-specific training material than English, and the abstract says this municipal-domain summarization task has been largely unexplored. That means researchers cannot simply assume that general summarization systems already know the document style, local-government vocabulary, or subject boundaries. The bottleneck is evidence: without high-quality manually crafted summaries, it is difficult to train systems or judge whether their outputs are faithful.
naive: A smart beginner might try to summarize each meeting by taking the first few sentences, extracting sentences with frequent words, or asking a general language model to shorten the whole document. Each shortcut misses the paper's target. Opening sentences may contain procedure rather than the actual substance. Frequent words can identify broad topics but not the decision or discussion outcome. Whole-document shortening can blur several agenda items into one mixed account. Even a fluent language model can sound convincing while omitting the exact subject-level facts citizens need. The deeper failure is that there is no trusted yardstick: without paired human summaries for each discussion subject, researchers cannot tell whether a system has learned municipal summarization or only produced plausible civic-sounding text.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn an under-specified public-document problem into a concrete learning and evaluation object. Instead of saying only that municipal minutes should be easier to read, it builds a corpus where each discussion subject has a manually written short summary. That pairing gives the field a set of examples: here is the long formal material, and here is the concise human version that preserves the point. The dataset contains 120 documents and 2,880 summaries, which implies the work is organized around many subject-level units inside meeting records. The authors then use the corpus to establish baseline results. They test generative summarization models such as BART and PRIMERA, as well as large language models, and evaluate outputs with wording-based and meaning-based metrics named in the abstract. The core idea is therefore infrastructure: make the task measurable before expecting better municipal summarizers.
mech: The mechanism begins with municipal meeting minutes in European Portuguese. Each document is a formal record, but the paper's target unit is a distinct discussion subject inside that record. The first transformation is human annotation: for each such subject, someone writes a concise summary. This creates paired data: source meeting material on one side, human-written subject summary on the other. Once those pairs exist, automatic systems can be tested. A summarization model receives the municipal text for a subject, or the relevant document context as defined by the dataset, and generates a shorter version. The paper names two families of systems: state-of-the-art generative models such as BART and PRIMERA, and large language models. Their outputs are then compared with the manually written summaries. Some comparisons count shared wording through ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR; these ask whether important words and phrases overlap. Another comparison, BERTScore, estimates whether the generated and reference summaries are close in meaning even when wording differs. The output of the paper is not only generated summaries. It is the dataset itself plus baseline scores that tell future researchers what current systems can do on this municipal, subject-level, European Portuguese task.
math: The main mathematical idea is supervised comparison under compression. Compression means replacing a long record with a shorter one while trying to keep the information that matters. The dataset supplies examples of that desired replacement: each source subject is paired with a human-written target summary. A generative model learns from many such pairs by adjusting its internal settings so its produced text becomes closer to the target examples. In everyday terms, it repeatedly asks, "When this kind of formal discussion appears, what short wording usually preserves its point?" The evaluation metrics are also mathematical comparisons. ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR count overlapping words, word groups, or related wording patterns, so they reward summaries that reuse important surface material from the human reference. BERTScore compares meaning through learned numeric representations of words and sentences; the number is meant to say whether two differently worded summaries still express similar content. The tradeoff is wording fidelity versus meaning flexibility. Word-overlap scores can punish a good paraphrase, while meaning scores can be too forgiving if a fluent sentence drifts away from a civic detail. Using both kinds helps expose different errors.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader text-mining and sequence themes because it treats language as ordered evidence that must be shortened without losing the point. It sits near other summarization work, but its pressure is different from web search or workplace analytics: the text is a public record, the language is European Portuguese, and the useful unit is a municipal discussion subject. It also connects to low-resource language work because the abstract makes scarcity central. The problem is not only model design; it is the absence of task-specific examples and trusted references. Finally, it touches evaluation, a recurring issue across language-model papers. A system that writes fluent summaries is not automatically useful. The field needs shared data and shared measurements before it can compare BART, PRIMERA, large language models, or later systems in a way that is more than anecdotal.
ww: The approach works because the dataset attacks the most basic missing piece: agreement about what the task is. Before CitiLink-Summ, a researcher could build a municipal summarizer, but the abstract says high-quality manually crafted summaries were scarce. That makes progress hard to measure. By pairing long formal material with human subject summaries, the paper gives models a signal about what should be kept and what can be left out. Subject-level pairing is especially important. Municipal meetings cover many items, so a single meeting-level summary could hide whether the system handled each item correctly. Baseline testing also helps because it turns general claims about modern summarizers into concrete behavior on this domain. If BART, PRIMERA, or large language models perform differently under lexical and semantic metrics, researchers can see whether errors are mostly wording mismatch, missing meaning, or poor handling of municipal document structure. The result is a clearer starting line for later improvements.
po: The payoff is a first benchmark for European Portuguese municipal-domain summarization. It gives future systems a public task shape: take dense meeting minutes and produce concise summaries for individual discussion subjects. The 120 documents and 2,880 hand-written summaries provide training and evaluation material where little existed before. The baseline results show how existing generative models and large language models behave on the task, using ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore. Practically, this can support tools that make local-government records easier for citizens to browse, while scientifically it lets researchers compare progress on a low-resource civic-document setting.
limits: The claims depend on the dataset representing the variety of European Portuguese municipal minutes that future systems will face. The abstract states the size, 120 documents and 2,880 summaries, but does not prove coverage across municipalities, topics, writing styles, or years. It also does not describe the annotation process in the provided text, so consistency among summary writers cannot be judged here. Automatic scores are useful but incomplete: word overlap and meaning similarity do not by themselves prove that a summary preserves legal nuance, dissent, or exact decisions. The paper establishes baselines, but the abstract does not show that deployed citizen-facing summaries are already trustworthy without human review.
